Compute a service table: expected years of service left

compute_service_table.Rd

For each value of a duration, such as age or years of service, estimates how many more years an employee in service at that duration stays, on average (ex).

It works like a life table. From estimate_decrement_rates() it takes the share of employees still in service a year later (px). It then follows an imaginary group of employees from the lowest duration to the highest, keeping a share px of them each year, and adds up the years they serve.

Usage

compute_service_table(personnel, ...)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
compute_service_table(
  personnel,
  duration_col,
  status_col = "employment_status",
  personnel_id_col = "personnel_id",
  ref_date_col = "ref_date",
  group_cols = NULL,
  include_all = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_dbi'
compute_service_table(
  personnel,
  duration_col,
  status_col = "employment_status",
  personnel_id_col = "personnel_id",
  ref_date_col = "ref_date",
  group_cols = NULL,
  include_all = TRUE,
  ...
)

# Default S3 method
compute_service_table(personnel, ...)

Arguments

personnel

A data frame, or a database table (tbl_dbi), with one row per person and snapshot.

...

Rarely needed settings:

  • smooth: TRUE to smooth the stay rates across durations first, which evens out durations with few people. Default FALSE.

  • span: how much to smooth; larger is smoother. Default 0.75.

  • radix: the size of the imaginary group. Default 100000. It only scales lx, Lx and Tx.

duration_col

The column of personnel to build the table on, in years: e.g. "age", or years of service from compute_tenure_panel(). Cut to whole years (2.9 counts as 2).

status_col

The employment status column. "active" means in service; any other value is a way of leaving.

personnel_id_col, ref_date_col

The person and snapshot date columns.

group_cols

Columns to build a separate table for, e.g. "gender", or NULL (the default) for one table.

include_all

TRUE (the default) for every column; FALSE for only the duration, the groups, px and ex.

Value

A service_table: a data.table with one row per group and duration, from the lowest to the highest seen. plot() draws it.

pop

People in service at that duration, whom px is measured on. NA where smoothing filled in a missing duration.

px

The share of them still in service a year later.

lx, lx_next

How many of the imaginary group are in service at that duration, and a year later.

Lx

Years they serve in that year (someone who leaves counts half).

Tx

Years they serve from that duration to the end of the table.

ex

Expected years of service left: Tx / lx.

Details

Not a forecast. The table assumes someone meets, at every later duration, the stay rates seen at that duration in your data. To project your own workforce, apply estimate_decrement_rates() to it year by year.

One snapshot a year. px is read as the chance of staying a year, so with monthly data, keep one month a year first.

Missing durations. People with no duration_col are left out, with a warning. If a whole duration is missing in a group (no one in service at it), every group's rates are smoothed to fill the gap, with a warning.

Where it ends. The table stops at the highest duration seen, so ex counts no service after it. If everyone at some duration left, no one is left after it: ex is NA from there, with a warning.

See also

estimate_decrement_rates() for the rates of each way of leaving.

Examples

st <- compute_service_table(bra_hrmis_personnel, "age", smooth = TRUE)
subset(st, age %in% c(25, 40, 55), select = c(age, px, ex))
#>      age        px        ex
#>    <int>     <num>     <num>
#> 1:    25 0.9052762 15.471887
#> 2:    40 0.9687776 15.068774
#> 3:    55 0.9152548  7.734391
plot(st)
